source.title: Detecting (Un)answerability in Large Language Models with Linear Directions
source.authors: Maor Juliet Lavi; T. Milo; Mor Geva

record.tranche_reason: The study uses difference-in-means directions and activation steering to detect and control unanswerability, drawing on prior work that includes refusal directions. It does not test safety refusal on harmful or harmless requests.
record.gate_note: The target behavior is abstention when an extractive-QA context cannot answer a question, not safety refusal. The causal abstention results are recorded under versions ["none"], rather than treated as tests of the refusal claim. Benchmark classification results concern unanswerability detection, not the claim's safety-refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the difference-in-means plus steering recipe (citing Arditi et al.) to find an unanswerability direction for extractive QA abstention. It never measures safety refusal of harmful vs. harmless instructions, so its results don't bear on any version. Its causal results concern a related but different construct (context-insufficiency abstention), recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that a single difference-in-means direction, selected by steering, captures unanswerability. It classifies unanswerable inputs and generalizes across datasets better than a trained classifier, especially after threshold calibration. It transfers partly to SelfAware and CREPE, and adding or subtracting it controls abstention. They make no claim about safety refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means and activation steering, but for answerability rather than safety refusal. Interventions are at one selected layer and position, not an ablation across every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected layer and position vary by model and dataset; the paper reports that the score threshold varies across evaluation datasets. Steering strength α changes abstention rates.

fits_no_version.finding: A single difference-in-means unanswerability direction is selected at one layer and position by steering. Adding it (α=2) raises abstention to about 96% on both answerable and unanswerable QA inputs. Negative α (−2) lowers abstention to 2.0% (answerable) and 19.4% (unanswerable). This holds in Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Gemma-3-12B-IT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abstention due to insufficient context in extractive QA is mediated by a linear difference-in-means direction that can causally induce or suppress abstention.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The reported causal abstention rates are means across datasets and are not broken out by model in the prose. The study evaluates abstention on extractive-QA inputs rather than safety refusal or general capability.
record.rows_left_out: Classification benchmarks, cross-dataset scores, and prompt-baseline results are omitted because they measure unanswerability detection or abstention in extractive QA, not safety refusal. The two-direction classification experiment in §C is likewise about unanswerability, not refusal.

untested.parts: Safety-refusal direction (harmful minus harmless): ablation removing refusal, addition inducing it, capability retention.
Multi-direction or cone structure of safety refusal. The two-direction test in §C concerns unanswerability only.
Transfer across languages or model variants. Cross-dataset transfer here is for unanswerability, not refusal.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Arditi et al. only as inspiration. The 'ablating' in the abstract is actually negative-α addition at a single layer and position. No capability-preservation check is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction mediates safety refusal, and whether removing or adding it changes safety refusal and preserves general capability.
Weight-edit ablation of refusal directions in released models.
Whether jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction, or training against its ablation adds robustness.
Whether safety refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or involves multiple refusal directions.
Whether harmfulness judgments are encoded separately from safety-refusal decisions.
Transfer of a safety-refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
How refusal training affects whether a removable safety-refusal direction exists.
Whether the safety-refusal direction claim holds in reasoning models.
